meta.title: How to Fail at Almost Everything and Still Win Big: Kind of the Story of My Life
meta.author: Scott Adams

parts.title: The Time I Was Crazy
parts.body: In 2005, Scott Adams was diagnosed with a mental illness by his doctor and a psychologist after he lost the ability to speak to humans, though he could speak normally to his cat or when alone. He declined Valium, not feeling crazy, but understood the diagnosis as his behavior appeared abnormal. His symptoms included his vocal cords clenching on certain consonants, making speech unintelligible, and a profound sense of loneliness from being unable to communicate. Adams, a professional speaker and syndicated cartoonist for Dilbert, faced a scheduled speaking event, risking humiliation in front of a thousand people. He informed his client and decided to go through with it to understand the pattern of his voice in that context.

parts.title: The Day of the Talk & Passion Is Bullshit
parts.body: The speaker faced a terrifying moment backstage before a talk, struggling to speak to organizers due to a voice problem. Despite his vast experience, he wondered if he could even deliver the speech. As he walked on stage, his heart pounded, but he managed to start speaking, though his voice was raspy. The audience loved his talk, but the moment he left the stage, his ability to speak vanished again, confirming the problem was in his brain. This experience fueled his three-year search for a solution, which forms the core of the book about turning failure into success. He then delves into the idea that passion is often misleading. He recalls his boss advising against lending money to passionate entrepreneurs, preferring those who work hard on spreadsheet-approved ventures. He hypothesizes that while passionate people might achieve huge successes, they also have many failures. He argues that success often *causes* passion, rather than the other way around. parts.title: My Spectacular Failure and the Birth of My Systems Mindset
parts.body: In CHAPTER FIVE: My Absolute Favorite Spectacular Failure, the author recounts a college experience combining bad luck, ignorance, and stupidity. On the way to an accounting firm interview in a half-blizzard, he made two crucial errors: no jacket and no suit and tie, thinking his college status was enough. The interviewer immediately dismissed him, pointing out his inappropriate attire. The "bad luck" element unfolded on the drive home when his engine died on a new highway in the Catskill Mountains during zero-degree Fahrenheit weather. Stranded without a jacket or cell phone, he faced a worst-case scenario, running for help as the cold threatened his life. Fearing a frozen death sleep, he vowed to trade his car for a one-way ticket to California if he survived. A traveling shoe salesman saved him, driving him back to campus. Months later, he kept his promise, trading his car for a ticket to northern California, a decision he calls the smartest he ever made. This near-death experience, triggered by his earlier failures, became his inspiration to move. He concludes with gratitude for the failure, stating he no longer fears death outdoors. In CHAPTER SIX: Goals Versus Systems, the author, at twenty-one with a college diploma, flew to California for the first time, seeking success away from his small hometown. Following his older brother Dave's earlier move, his plan was to stay with Dave and find a banking job. He traded his old car for a one-way ticket and, mistakenly believing it was standard, wore his first real suit for the flight, fearing being denied boarding for improper dress. He also worried about keeping it wrinkle-free for job interviews. On the plane, he met a CEO of a screw company who offered him career advice: always look for a better job, making job seeking an ongoing process rather than a reactive one. This was his first exposure to the idea of a system over a goal. The CEO, who had job-hopped to success, exemplified this by focusing on continuous improvement rather than specific job titles. The author learned that appearance matters, as his suit earned him a potential job offer from the CEO, which wouldn't have happened if he'd dressed casually. He observes that systems-driven people generally do better than goal-oriented people, who often feel in a continuous state of failure until their goal is met, and then feel empty afterward. Systems, he argues, provide a continuous sense of accomplishment and maintain personal energy. He defines a goal as a specific, future objective and a system as a regular activity increasing long-term happiness, emphasizing that systems have no deadlines and offer a more consistent path to success, as seen in examples like Mark Zuckerberg and Warren Buffett.

parts.title: From Corporate Conflict to Cartooning: The Power of Deciding, Enlightened Selfishness, and Energy Management
parts.body: The author discusses a workplace conflict where he applied company policy strictly regarding smoking, leading to a temporary walkout and the expectation of being fired. He highlights his attraction to controversy. Ultimately, his boss's boss intervened, making most offices smoke-free and requiring smokers in senior management to close their doors, a result the author considered ideal. Later, his career at Pacific Bell was hindered by a diversity policy preventing the promotion of white males, leading him to feel a sense of unwanted freedom and to explore new paths. This led him to cartooning, despite a lack of artistic talent. He started practicing drawing and using affirmations, specifically: "I, Scott Adams, will be a famous cartoonist." The author introduces Chapter Nine: Deciding Versus Wanting, emphasizing that success requires paying a price. He contrasts wishing with deciding, noting that deciding leads to action. He then introduces Chapter Ten: The Selfishness Illusion, arguing for enlightened selfishness as beneficial to society, citing examples like taxes and job creation. He provides permission to prioritize self-care, which ultimately benefits others. Finally, Chapter Eleven: The Energy Metric suggests organizing life around maximizing personal energy to better manage multiple priorities. He defines this as calm, focused energy and explains how it improves work quality, speed, and personal life, using the analogy of a "Dog Whisperer" for human interaction. He also contrasts simplifiers (like himself) with optimizers (like his wife Shelly), highlighting how simplification frees up time and energy, which he considers a "superpower" for his cartooning career. He concludes by recommending matching mental state to activity, using specific sitting positions for work, maintaining tidiness, and overcoming the fear of not knowing through quick research.

parts.title: The Asshole Lifestyle and Prioritizing Personal Energy
parts.body: Being an asshole can pollute group energy and is often seen as a lifestyle choice like "being yourself." However, this behavior can have a cost to your personal energy due to blowback and wasted effort in cleaning up messes. Many people adopt this "asshole lifestyle," and it's gender-inclusive, encompassing selfishness, arrogance, mean-spiritedness, and other flaws. The author defines an asshole as someone who unpleasantly impacts others' lives without productive or necessary reasons. Behaviors include changing the subject to oneself, dominating conversations, bragging, cheating, lying, disagreeing with everything, using honesty as cruelty, withholding favors, and abandoning civil behavior. Asshole behavior might feel good in the short term, like an addiction, but it's a bad long-term trade-off for personal well-being. The author suggests thinking of priorities in concentric circles: you (health) at the center, then economics (job, investments), followed by family, friends, and lovers. Outer rings include local community, country, and the world. The key is to manage inner circles before focusing on outer ones. Life isn't simple, and priorities overlap and conflict. A simple rule is to judge options by their influence on your personal energy: choices that make you stressed, unhealthy, and drained are likely wrong, while right choices usually charge you up. Meaningful work, even if demanding, can be energizing, unlike brain-deadening tasks. The author clarifies that priorities aren't about what you love most, but what you need to get right for the things you love to thrive. Even bad choices can temporarily energize, but long-term negative consequences are often obvious.

parts.title: My Speaking Career & The Path to Success
parts.body: The author shares how a smart friend helped him start a speaking career. Initially hesitant, he was advised to ask for $5,000 for a speech, expecting to be rejected. To his surprise, the offer was immediately accepted, including first-class travel and hotel. As his cartoon, *Dilbert*, grew in popularity, his speaking fees steadily increased from $10,000 to $45,000, with one offer reaching $100,000. This success highlights the value of knowing different things from your friends, not just CEOs. After six months of losing his voice in 2005, the author was frustrated by the nameless problem. Doctors couldn't diagnose it, so he turned to the Internet. A sudden connection between his previous hand problem (focal dystonia) and his voice issue led him to search for "voice dystonia." He found spasmodic dysphonia, a condition where vocal cords clench involuntarily. A video confirmed it was his exact voice pattern. With a name, he found an expert doctor who confirmed the diagnosis but stated there was no cure. The author, an optimist, saw this as a challenge to find his own cure and help others. The standard treatment for spasmodic dysphonia is Botox injections into the vocal cords, a creepy and inconsistent process. The author tried it for a few months; the first shot helped him speak at his wedding but wore off quickly. Subsequent shots were ineffective and unpredictable due to varying doses and injection accuracy. He decided to stop Botox because it masked the effects of other potential treatments, opting to seek a lasting fix despite becoming essentially voiceless without it. The author discusses how to recognize your talents and when to quit. He focuses on ordinary talents that combine to create something extraordinary, suggesting that childhood obsessions (like his compulsive doodling) and tolerance for risk (like drawing inappropriate comics despite potential punishment) can indicate natural aptitudes. He contrasts this with skills he enjoyed but didn't obsess over, like riding a motorcycle, where the risk eventually outweighed the joy. He emphasizes that successful ventures often start out well and gain immediate traction, even if the initial product is flawed (e.g., early cell phones, *The Simpsons*, *Dilbert*). He learned in Hollywood that strong reactions from a subset of the public (the "x factor") are a better predictor of success than average approval. If your work doesn't excite anyone, it's time to move on; if it does, be prepared to fight for it. The author observes a three-year-old intensely practicing tennis, demonstrating a natural impulse to practice. This contrasts with his own experiences practicing economically useless skills like spinning a basketball. He argues that people are either natural "practicers" or find repetition torturous, and this inclination won't change. Therefore, it's crucial to craft a life plan that aligns with one's natural inclinations. If you're not a natural practicer, avoid careers requiring endless repetition and instead pursue professions that reward novelty-seeking and skill-building through ever-changing experiences (e.g., architect, programmer), which he calls the "more fun cousin of practice." The author critiques schools for not teaching systems of success. He proposes a Success Formula: "Every Skill You Acquire Doubles Your Odds of Success." He clarifies that this doesn't mean excellence, but rather being "merely good" at multiple skills (Good + Good > Excellent). He uses an analogy of pruning a résumé for $100 per word to illustrate how an inaccurate but simple formula can effectively guide behavior. He sees himself as an example: mediocre art, business, and writing skills, combined with early Internet knowledge and a good sense of humor, became a powerful market force. His business background provided fodder for *Dilbert* and helped market it, particularly by putting his email in the strip and focusing on workplace humor based on reader feedback. He concludes that quantity often beats quality when it comes to skills.

parts.title: The Knowledge Formula: The More You Know, the More You Can Know
parts.body: The author emphasizes the importance of continuous learning and diversifying knowledge across various fields, likening new concepts to understanding a zebra after knowing what a horse is. He advocates for daily news consumption from diverse topics like business, health, and science to identify patterns and build a foundation for future learning. The key is to start with interesting topics to make news reading enjoyable, gradually expanding to other areas, making learning feel easy and natural. He cautions against dwelling on negative news, preferring stories about hopeful topics like green technology. The author reads news not for "truth" but to broaden exposure and make his brain more efficient, viewing it as a source of energy and optimism rather than just information.

parts.title: Business Writing and Accounting
parts.body: Learning business writing was a game-changer. It's all about getting to the point and cutting out unnecessary words and passive voice. These techniques make your writing clearer, more persuasive, and even funnier. For example, removing a word like “already” often doesn't change the meaning but makes the sentence stronger. Also, using direct writing (like “The boy hit the ball”) is much easier for the brain to process than passive constructions. Mastering these simple rules can make you seem smarter and more effective in communication. Accounting is crucial for being an effective adult, even if it seems boring. Understanding basic accounting concepts, like cash-flow projections and the time value of money, is part of the vocabulary of business. Many businesses fail because operators lack this fundamental understanding, prioritizing culinary skill over financial viability. Even if you pay others to handle accounting, you need enough knowledge to check their work and understand the basics to make informed decisions.

parts.title: Understanding Theory vs. Hypothesis & The Art of Persuasion
parts.body: This text distinguishes between theory and hypothesis, noting that a theory is a well-tested scientific explanation, while a hypothesis is an unproven idea. The author humorously admits to misusing "theory" in casual conversation, leading to public complaints. The text then transitions to the art of persuasion, emphasizing its importance in everyday interactions, whether in sales, personal relationships, or professional settings. The author suggests reading books on persuasion to understand its depth and effectiveness, highlighting it as a powerful skill that should be used judiciously and ethically. Key persuasive words and phrases are introduced, such as "Because" (which makes requests seem more reasonable), "Would you mind…?" (which signals a considerate request), "I’m not interested" (an effective conversation-stopper), and "I don’t do that" (a firm rule-like refusal). Other tactics include using "I have a rule…" to politely decline, "I just wanted to clarify…" to indirectly address difficult statements, and "Is there anything you can do for me?" to appeal to someone's helpful nature. The importance of a high-quality "Thank you", with specific details, is stressed, likening it to a dog treat that encourages future cooperation. Finally, sharing a non-dangerous secret with the phrase "This is just between you and me" is presented as a fast-track way to build trust and friendship.

parts.title: Happiness
parts.body: This chapter is about happiness. The author believes the only reasonable goal in life is to maximize your total lifetime experience of happiness. This isn't selfish, as normal people need to treat others well to be happy. Understanding what happiness is and how it works is crucial, similar to understanding gardening to grow a successful garden. Happiness is defined as a feeling from pleasant sensations produced by your body chemistry. It's not as dependent on circumstances as often thought; for example, amputees often return to their previous happiness levels. Everyone has a limited range of happiness, and life circumstances only jiggle them within that range. The good news is that most people can spend more time at the top of their personal range. The author treats himself like a "moist robot" and manipulates his body chemistry for happiness, which he sees as 80% of the solution. While pills and drugs can alter mood, he advocates a more natural approach. The biggest trick is being able to do what you want, when you want. Timing is more important than intrinsic value; a mediocre meal when starving is better than an extraordinary meal when full. Controlling your schedule is key, as flexibility contributes more to happiness than wealth. Parents understand this, as kids remove much schedule flexibility, impacting their happiness despite loving their children.

parts.title: Quitting Diet Coke and the Science of Eating
parts.body: The author used to consume a large amount of Diet Coke but decided to quit as an experiment for this book. The first week was challenging, but by substituting coffee, the need for willpower was greatly reduced. After eight weeks, the cravings were completely gone, and the author now feels more alert throughout the day. This experiment suggests that cravings can be managed and eliminated with a strategic approach, even for long-standing habits. Regarding healthy eating, the author emphasizes that it needs to be convenient to be sustainable. There's a lot of uncertainty in nutrition science, and what's considered healthy can change frequently. The author suggests using your body as a laboratory to test different foods and observe their effects on your energy and mood. This personal experimentation, combined with insights from science, can help you identify patterns that work best for your individual body.

parts.title: Vegetarianism, Coffee, and Fitness as Systems
parts.body: This section discusses the author's vegetarian diet, emphasizing it's a choice, not a burden. He feels lucky not to overeat and enjoys the option of guilt-free treats later. He notes that being vegetarian is easier in California than in places like Kansas City, where he once received beef gravy on fries and bacon bits on salad when ordering vegetarian options. He concludes that the inconvenience is paid for by feeling good physically and the "holier-than-thou" sensation, asserting that becoming vegetarian is easier than it looks. The author then shifts to the benefits of coffee, recommending two to four cups a day for increased alertness, happiness, and productivity. Coffee can also encourage exercise and contains antioxidants that reduce the risk of stroke, Parkinson's, dementia, abnormal heart rhythms, type 2 diabetes, and certain cancers. He describes coffee as a tool that literally makes him enjoy work, requiring no willpower. It helps manage energy levels, leading to higher highs and lower lows energy-wise, which he uses to his advantage, saving "dull-brain hours" for simple tasks. The main downside is caffeine addiction and "coffee headaches," but he argues its benefits for peak mental performance make it highly recommendable, even feeling sorry for those who haven't adopted the habit. The "Pleasure Unit Hypothesis" posits that happier individuals care less about food taste, making healthy eating easier. He illustrates this by suggesting one would choose a dream destination over favorite food if the destination offered other pleasures. The idea is that getting your entire life in order simplifies maintaining an ideal weight. This creates a circular problem: good health improves life, and a good life makes healthy choices easier. He includes diet and fitness in his success book because health impacts success, and success without health isn't enjoyable. The section concludes with "The Healthy Eating Summary," a nine-point system for no-willpower dieting which includes paying attention to energy levels, removing unhealthy food from the home, stocking convenient healthy options, avoiding addictive foods (white rice, potatoes, desserts, white bread, fried foods), eating healthy food freely, getting enough sleep to avoid false hunger, using fatty healthy foods for tiredness-induced hunger, choosing low-calorie healthy options for social eating, and learning to season bland healthy foods. The author emphasizes that this system helps lose cravings without sacrifice, leading to long-term success without relying on willpower, which he deems a "losing strategy" for weight loss. The next section, "Fitness," starts with the author's childhood experience of being constantly active through sports and physical play. As an adult, exercise became difficult due to life getting in the way. He found it hard to make time and enjoy it, recalling painful soccer games and failed attempts at running. He acknowledges that exercise is hard work, and with marriage and kids, it can become impractical. Despite trying "nearly every exercise tip, trick, and fad," he condenses all fitness advice into one sentence: "Be Active Every Day." He admits this sounds useless but promises a simpler, more effective approach, likening simplification to why people brush their teeth easily but put off complex tasks. He argues that complexity in any life area (exercise, diet, career, finance, social life) borrows willpower from other areas. For young people, regular exercise is easier, but for adults, it often becomes the first thing sacrificed when busy. His challenge is to convince the reader that "being active every day" naturally brings together all fitness elements without relying on willpower. He states that any exercise requiring willpower is unsustainable, advocating for starting with levels that "don't feel like work." This approach leads to gradual, natural increases in activity because it feels easy and good, turning boredom into a tool. He explains that dedicated exercisers don't like missing a day, which is the desired state: when fitness becomes a daily habit that the body and brain prefer, requiring no willpower. He contrasts this with the "illusion" of willpower in long-distance runners, suggesting they have a genetic gift that makes running enjoyable for them. He dismisses the idea of adopting exercise plans meant for different body types and brains, emphasizing the need for a natural, easy evolution into a routine that works for the individual without willpower. He notes the overwhelming amount of exercise advice online, criticizing most for requiring willpower, which he views as a "losing strategy." His preferred approach is simple and willpower-free, arguing that being active daily actually *increases* energy. He defines "active" ambiguously, making it a system, not a goal. Unlike a specific goal (e.g., "Run ten miles every day"), "being active in some way every day" is achievable for everyone, from playing basketball to cleaning the garage. The key is the "every day" part, from which everything else naturally springs. He also touches on how market forces complicate fitness with endless, intimidating questions about workouts, diets, and rest, which are only practical for serious athletes or those with ample free time. He then addresses the challenge of scheduling exercise in a marriage, illustrating how conflicts arise with a spouse's schedule. He offers three practical solutions: 1) join an organized team (because the schedule is set by a third party, it feels less personal to the spouse), 2) always exercise at the same time every day (creating a predictable "system" that feels less like a conscious choice to be unavailable), and 3) exercise together (if both are genuinely committed). He uses his own example of exercising at lunchtime due to its predictability, contrasting it with the unsuccessful method of exercising "whenever you have some spare time." The author's system for motivation includes maintaining energy through diet and the rule to never over-exercise to the point of not wanting to be active the next day. The "right amount of exercise today is whatever amount makes me look forward to being active tomorrow." He criticizes the "no pain, no gain" mentality, arguing that excessive effort uses up willpower needed for other areas (like avoiding unhealthy food) and that soreness acts as a "penalty," making people quit. Instead, light exercise provides immediate rewards like stress reduction and energy boost, naturally leading to increased activity over time. He emphasizes that to form a habit, exercise must be done "every day without fail," as rest days break the pattern. He rewards himself after exercise with healthy snacks, reading, or coffee, creating a strong positive association. He highlights coffee's role in boosting athletic performance and willingness to put in effort, suggesting it for those struggling to exercise. He also mentions using ibuprofen (with a doctor's consultation) to manage soreness and ensure readiness for the next day's activity. To overcome days of low motivation, he suggests a trick using "cues" or "keys." Instead of forcing a vigorous workout, he grants himself 100% permission *not* to exercise but still puts on his exercise clothes and shoes. The physical act of getting ready triggers a "going-to-the-gym subroutine" in his brain, boosting his energy. He then drives to the gym, looks around, and assesses his mood, maintaining the option to leave without working out. He states that 95% of the time, this sequence leads him to exercise, improving his mood. The few times he leaves without working out, he considers it a win because he used his system, rather than a failure (which is for those with *goals*). This approach ensures his attitude improves regardless, and he at least gets out and clears his head. He advises not to worry about the amount of exercise on a given day, as the key is making it a daily habit. He notes studies indicating moderate exercise is best for longevity and that variety and challenge will naturally increase over time. He then brings up the "Hair-Care Death Spiral," referencing Dr. Regina M. Benjamin's observation that women skip exercise due to hair-related issues. He argues that prioritizing hair over health is a "loser strategy." He posits three reasons women want great hair (attracting partners, career, feeling good about self), all of which relate to influencing others. From a heterosexual male perspective, he asserts, "We Prefer You Healthy," stating no man would prefer an unhealthy woman with great hair over a fit one with a ponytail. He also argues that healthier-looking applicants have a subconscious bias in hiring. He suggests that if hair care is for feeling good, a healthy body always trumps a good hairdo. He advises women caught in the "hair-care death spiral" to reframe their thinking: if skipping exercise for hair, they are actively choosing to become less attractive, less employable, and less healthy in the long term. He concludes by contrasting short-term hair goals with fitness as a system, stating, "Systems are for winners."

parts.title: A Final Note About Affirmations
parts.body: This chapter is about affirmations and how they appear to have a beneficial value, even if their mechanism isn't fully understood by science. The author acknowledges that some might see this as magic or psychic powers, but suggests they are likely a phenomenon of the mind, impacting psychology and perception. Affirmations could influence the brain through focus, motivation, or chemical reactions, similar to other forms of positive thinking like prayers or visualization. The author notes that in his experience, affirmations seem to have more power than simple positive thinking, creating an "illusion" that the world is changing to satisfy them. The author offers several explanations for the apparent power of affirmations: selective memory (remembering successes, forgetting failures), the possibility that people reporting success are liars (though he asserts he isn't), false memory (remembering events differently), and that optimists (who often practice affirmations) notice more opportunities than pessimists. He also suggests that perhaps only those who deep down believe in their talent bother with affirmations, or that our brains create illusions for survival benefits. He even touches on the idea of humans being holograms in a computer simulation, where affirmations could be a form of programming code. Ultimately, he reiterates that he has no objective information on their effectiveness but believes they involve a deep and consistent focus on what you want. He clarifies that affirmations, when viewed as a system for focus, optimism, and validation, are consistent with his "systems for winners" philosophy, recommending broad objectives.
